# Fine-tuning a small embedding model for Swiss federal law: what worked, what didn't, and a bug in my own numbers

> This is not an official publication. Only the publication by the Federal Chancellery is authoritative. Dies ist keine amtliche Veröffentlichung. Massgebend ist allein die Veröffentlichung durch die Bundeskanzlei. Not legal advice.

*Francisco Mira. Code, benchmark, model and every number below: [github.com/franciscomira/fedlex-rag-benchmark](https://github.com/franciscomira/fedlex-rag-benchmark). The model is on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/franciscomira/fedlex-e5-small).*

I wanted to answer one question with measurements instead of opinions: **can a small fine-tuned model replace an LLM call in a cross-lingual legal retrieval pipeline, at lower cost and latency?** The answer I got is "mostly yes for finding the right article, and I can't tell it apart from the LLM pipeline on answer quality", with a list of reasons not to trust that too far. This post is the argument, the numbers, and the places where I was wrong.

## The setting

Swiss federal law is published officially in German, French and Italian, as parallel texts, and the same article keeps the same number in all three. That makes a clean experiment: the content stays fixed and only the language changes. I took 8 federal acts (the Code of Obligations, the Civil Code and six others), 4,073 articles in three languages, and wrote a benchmark of 242 items: questions in English, German, French and Italian, each with the one article (sometimes two) that answers it, plus questions that the law does not answer, where the right behaviour is to say so.

English questions are the hard case on purpose. No article is in English, so an English question over German, French and Italian text is cross-lingual in every configuration.

Two rules shaped everything. First, **measure before changing**: every change to the pipeline is judged by an evaluation harness, never by looking at a few outputs. Second, **the model never touches what must be exact**: article ids, SR numbers and citations are produced and validated by code. The model may rank passages and draft an answer; code checks every cited id against the articles that were actually retrieved, and an id the model invents is dropped and counted.

I split the benchmark into a development part and a test part. I chose configurations on the development part, froze them, and ran each frozen configuration on the test part once. The test set has 164 answerable questions in about 110 independent groups (a question and its translations count once), so intervals are wide. Every number below has a 95% bootstrap interval that resamples those groups, and I say which differences I cannot claim.

## Where this sits

Two pieces of earlier work are close. SCALE (Stern et al.) is a multi-task Swiss legal benchmark whose retrieval task takes the facts of a court case as the query and looks for the laws it cites. ZHAW's JuRAG tested twelve multilingual embedding models on court decisions, with twenty-six questions in four languages, and found the embedding model to be the biggest lever. My setting differs: short natural-language questions answered by one statute article, cited answers scored for faithfulness and for refusing when the law is silent, and cost and latency per query. Their finding about embeddings fits what I saw. They also report that LLM paraphrasing of queries made retrieval worse, while my LLM translation of English questions into the language of the text helped a lot; those are different operations on different collections, and I did not test why. I read both from their published task descriptions and blog post, not their results tables, and I don't compare numbers with theirs.

## What I thought the problem was, and what it was

I started with a different question: whether a small fine-tuned *reranker* could match a frontier LLM reranker. The first baseline made that question uninteresting. On the development questions (a window of thirty candidates, with my first-round embedder, never repeated after the fix below), a small and cheap LLM reranker and a much larger one brought the right article into the top ten equally often, at prices that differed by about twenty times. Once the right article is among the candidates, a decent reranker seems to find it. The benchmark probably can't tell rerankers apart, partly because the questions were written from the article text, but I only showed that on that one setup.

What the baseline did show is that **the first search step is the bottleneck**. A plain hybrid search (keywords plus a multilingual embedding model) found the right article in the top ten for only 0.14 [0.05, 0.25] of English questions, against 0.58 [0.44, 0.72] for German (measured with an embedder bug that I describe below; corrected, English is 0.24 [0.12, 0.37]). Asking a small LLM to translate the question into German, French and Italian before searching, and reranking, lifted English to 0.71 [0.57, 0.86] (same broken embedder; 0.86 [0.74, 0.95] after the fix). That works, but it costs an LLM call and several seconds per question.

So I changed the question: **can a small fine-tuned embedding model close the gap that LLM translation closes, with no LLM call at query time?** I did not fine-tune a reranker. The original question stays open.

## A bug in my own measurements

Before the fine-tuning results, the correction, because it changes how much of the earlier numbers you should believe.

My embedding code averaged padding tokens into the vectors of texts that were embedded in a batch. A question embedded alone was right; every passage of the index was embedded in a batch and was subtly wrong. I found it by accident: the same untrained model scored much better in a separate validation script than in my pipeline. After the fix, the untuned hybrid search on the test questions went from 0.49 to 0.55 recall@10 (paired difference +0.055 [+0.009, +0.104]), and English from 0.14 [0.05, 0.25] to 0.24 [0.12, 0.37]. Every first-round number that I re-measured (the plain search, the search with a reranker, and the translation pipeline, retrieval only) went up, and I had written conclusions on top of the old ones. I added an errata section to the earlier report and marked what I could not re-run: the first round's answer-quality numbers were measured on the broken first stage, and the agent experiment and the development reranker comparison were never repeated, so I don't know in which direction their gaps would move.

## Fine-tuning

I fine-tuned `multilingual-e5-small` (118 million parameters). For training data I had a small LLM write four questions for each of 3,200 articles that are not in the benchmark (a pool of 3,201, of which one failed validation): two in English and two in German, French or Italian, in six deliberately different styles (a lay description of a situation, legal wording, keywords, a third party asking, and so on). I trained on the questions of 2,876 of those articles and kept the rest for validation: 11,504 training questions, for 0.87 USD of generation. I removed every development and test answer article, every article next to one, and near-duplicates of them, and wrote tests that fail if any of them leaks in.

Training used a standard in-batch ranking loss, three epochs, on a free Kaggle GPU in under 15 minutes. The whole phase, with data generation, audits and test runs, cost 2.16 USD in API calls. Two findings I did not expect: a quarter of the data gives most of the gain, and mining hard negatives, the textbook improvement, gave no claimable gain (+0.017 [0.000, +0.061] recall@10 on 58 development questions) and made each training step 1.7 times slower, so I dropped it.

## Do the answers get better?

Retrieval metrics say how often the right article is found. They do not say whether the answers are good, so I also measured answers with the pipeline that I would actually serve (P2): the tuned embedder as an int8 file (118 MB instead of 470 MB, runs on a CPU), a small LLM reranker over the best candidates, and a drafted answer whose citations are validated by code, with an explicit "not in the sources" path. Answers were scored by a separate judge model from another family. On 63 facts from a small sample it agreed 81% of the time with the labels of one reviewer, who reads English only and worked from machine English translations of the answers (kappa 0.61, just over the 80% bar I had set). That is good enough to compare systems and not good enough to read small differences, and the intervals below do not include judge noise.

| System | Recall@10 | Fact recall | Faithfulness | Traps handled (exact 95% interval) | Cost per question (USD) | Latency p50 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **P1** Fine-tuned embedder as int8 ONNX file, retrieval only | 0.79 [0.69, 0.88] | — | — | — | 0.0000 [0.0000, 0.0000] | 0.05 s |
| **P2** Full pipeline with cited answers (fine-tuned embedder, reranker, answerer) | 0.86 [0.78, 0.94] | 0.80 [0.71, 0.89] | 0.84 [0.80, 0.87] | 9 of 15 [0.32, 0.84] | 0.0024 [0.0023, 0.0025] | 5.4 s |
| **P3** Translation pipeline with the answer step | 0.87 [0.79, 0.94] | 0.82 [0.75, 0.89] | 0.85 [0.83, 0.88] | 11 of 15 [0.45, 0.92] | 0.0030 [0.0029, 0.0031] | 11.9 s |

- Fact recall, the share of the gold facts that the answer states, is 0.80 [0.71, 0.89] for the pipeline I serve (P2) and 0.82 [0.75, 0.89] for the LLM-translation pipeline with the same answer step (P3). P2 minus P3 is -0.021 [-0.099, +0.051]: not claimable. Recall@10 and faithfulness are likewise not distinguishable.
- P2 costs 0.0024 USD and takes 5.4 s per question (median), against 0.0030 USD and 11.9 s for P3: 20% cheaper, and 2.2 times faster at the median. Cost and latency differences are claimable in a paired comparison, but the two runs ran at the same time on one laptop on one day, so read the latency as relative. The paired mean difference in latency (P2 minus P3) is -6.061 [-6.502, -5.610] seconds.
- The int8 file is not free: against the full-precision model, MRR on the test set is -0.055 [-0.097, -0.018] (claimable) and recall@10 is -0.021 [-0.060, +0.012] (not claimable). A stop rule I had written in advance said to stop and ask if the int8 file lost a claimable amount of ranking quality; it did, I asked, and I kept it because the pipeline I serve puts a reranker on top. The MCP server's plain search tool and the local search demo do not, and serve the int8 ordering as it is.
- Citation precision, the share of cited articles that are the gold article, is 0.58 [0.50, 0.65] for P2 and 0.57 [0.49, 0.64] for P3, and citation recall is 0.88 [0.80, 0.95] and 0.88 [0.80, 0.94]. Part of the gap is that the models cite every article they used while the gold is one article, but I did not separate that from wrong citations.
- The agent from my first round (D: a planner, per-language searchers and a citation checker) reached recall@10 of 0.92 [0.87, 0.97] and fact recall of 0.81 [0.75, 0.86], even on the broken first stage, nominally above P2 on both (within the noise of each other). I never re-ran it. I do not claim that the pipeline I serve is the best system I built.
- Faithfulness stays near 0.84 [0.80, 0.87]: about one claim in six is not supported by the cited text, whatever the retrieval. On the trap questions, which the law does not answer, P2 handled 9 of 15 correctly and P3 11 of 15. That is too few questions to rank anything, and it is still the weakest part of every system I built.

A corrected 0.0000 USD, median 0.08 s; T1 0.0000 USD, median 0.07 s; T2 0.0016 USD, median 1.6 s; C' 0.0024 USD, median 8.0 s; P2 0.0024 USD, median 5.4 s; P3 0.0030 USD, median 11.9 s.](figures/fig_cost_latency.svg)

*Cost and speed per question.*

So the honest summary is: **a fine-tuned small model, trained on a free GPU for a phase that cost about two dollars in API calls, finds the right article in the top ten at 0.81 against 0.87 for an LLM translation pipeline: the difference is -0.064 [-0.149, +0.016], so the tuned model could be up to about fifteen points worse and is at most about two points better.** A pipeline built on it showed no detectable difference in answer quality from the LLM pipeline (fact recall -0.021 [-0.099, +0.051]), with the caveat that its fact recall could be up to about ten points lower, and that on fact recall, faithfulness and trap count the point estimates favour the LLM pipeline. What is solid is the cost and latency side: the tuned retrieval stage is free and fast, and the whole pipeline is cheaper and faster. Judge noise is not in these intervals.

## What I would not claim

- **The benchmark rewards what the model learned.** Every benchmark question was written by an LLM from the text of one article, and so were my training questions, by the same family of model. Part of the gain may be the model learning that writing style rather than cross-lingual retrieval. Real users' questions would be the real test, and I have none.
- **No expert has looked at any of it.** Nobody on the project reads German, French and Italian well enough to have reviewed the training questions, and no Swiss-law expert reviewed the benchmark, the gold facts or any answer. The single human reviewer reads English only and has no legal training.
- **The test set is small.** About 110 independent questions. Only large differences are claimable; I report the ones that are not as "not distinguishable", never as ties.
- **I changed several things at once.** Compared with my first-round pipeline, the retrieval stage differs in four ways at once: fine-tuning, the padding fix, no keyword search, and int8. The improvement in answer quality over my first-round single-shot system (B) is real in the data (+0.196 [+0.103, +0.293] fact recall, claimable); against my first-round translation system (C) it is +0.040 [-0.051, +0.130], not claimable. I can't say which of the four changes produced it.
- **Parts of the first round were never repeated:** the agent system and the trap results with the corrected first stage. They are marked as such on the results page.
- **The leakage check has a known gap.** I excluded near-duplicates of the test articles symmetrically, so a short training article that is contained in a long test article can slip through. I measured the effect: the gain of the tuned model over the untuned one holds on the test questions that are not touched by such articles, but the tuned model's absolute level on the touched ones may be flattered.
- **A reranker was never fine-tuned**, which was my original question.

## What I would do next

Put real questions from people who work with Swiss law into the test set, and have a lawyer who reads German, French and Italian review the gold answers and a sample of the training questions. Build harder negatives from neighbouring articles, because this benchmark is easy for rerankers by construction. And finally fine-tune the reranker I started with, now that the first stage is no longer the bottleneck.

## Try it, check it, break it

The [results page](https://franciscomira.github.io/fedlex-rag-benchmark/) rebuilds every table from the committed run folders with one command, and says for each number whether reproducing it needs API keys or a GPU. There is [a page of ten recorded answers](https://franciscomira.github.io/fedlex-rag-benchmark/examples.html), all ten kept, including one where the system refused a question the law answers in part. There is a four-tool MCP server for search, exact article lookup and cited answers; several Fedlex MCP servers already exist, and what this one adds is retrieval measured on a benchmark and citations validated by code, over only 8 acts. There is no live demo: when I tried to create a free Docker Space on Hugging Face, the API answered "402 Payment Required" (it needs a paid plan). I did not look for another host and did not want to put a paid model call behind a public endpoint, so the search demo runs locally.

The last phase, which covers the measurements of the pipeline above and shipping it, cost 4.2 USD of API calls.
